slides.label: Title
slides.notes: The biggest outcome on the course and the most practical. Every cadet needs a compass in hand for this lesson - watching someone else do it teaches nothing. Warn them now that they will be doing all of it themselves before the end.
slides.html:
2434 (Church Fenton) Squadron · Air Training Corps
Basic Navigation Using
Map and Compass
Learning Outcome 3
Using a lightweight compass for practical navigation — on the map and on the ground
Uncontrolled copy · not subject to amendment

slides.label: LO3 statement
slides.notes: Read it out. BE ABLE TO - this one is assessed by doing, not by answering. Say what that looks like: set a bearing off the map, walk it, and take a bearing off the ground and plot it.
slides.html:
Learning Outcome 3
Be able to use a lightweight compass for practical navigation

slides.label: Section: the compass
slides.notes: Signpost part one. Naming the parts feels dry but everything after this depends on the cadets and you meaning the same thing by the same words.
slides.html:
Part One
The compass
What the parts are called, what each one does, and how to look after it.

slides.label: Where compasses are used
slides.notes: Keep it to a minute. The point is that this is a serious instrument with a long pedigree, not a toy in the stores. If anyone has used one for orienteering, get them to say what it felt like under time pressure.
slides.html:
The compass
Five thousand years old and still the tool
On land
Hill walking, mountaineering, cycling, orienteering
Where you will use one.
At sea and under it
Sailing, scuba diving
Where a bearing is the only reference there is.
In the air and at work
Flying, surveying, military
Where the same principles scale up.
The compass was first discovered by the Chinese around five thousand years ago. They are now made for use on land, at sea, under it, and in the air.

slides.label: The Silva compass
slides.notes: Hold one up. Get every cadet to confirm they have the same thing in front of them - a protractor compass, not a button compass or a phone app. If your stores have mixed types, sort that out now rather than mid-exercise.
slides.html:
The compass
The Silva-style compass
There are many styles of compass. In the Air Cadets we use a Silva-style baseplate compass.
▸A clear baseplate you can see the map through
▸A rotating housing, or capsule, marked in degrees
▸A magnetic needle floating in liquid
▸Scales along the edge for measuring on the map
Every part named — learn these words

slides.label: ANIMATION Parts of the Compass
slides.notes: Run this before the two naming slides, not after. Let it play through once without commentary, then run it again and pause on each part while cadets point to that part on their own compass. That second pass is where the names stick.
slides.anim: Nav LO3 - Parts of the Compass.html
slides.html:
Animation · play now
Parts of the Compass
The whole compass taken apart piece by piece — baseplate, housing, needle, direction of travel arrow, index line, orienting lines and scale — each one named and held on screen.
Open the animation →
Also in the library: all 18 navigation animations

slides.label: Baseplate housing needle
slides.notes: Make them say the words back. The commonest confusion is calling the housing the dial or the bezel interchangeably - decide on your terms and stick to them. Point out that the needle is the only part that is magnetic; everything else is just geometry.
slides.html:
Parts of the compass
The three parts you can see moving
▸Baseplate — the mounting for the housing. Carries the scales and rulers.
▸Compass housing — holds the needle and carries the degree markings on a rotating bezel.
▸The needle — a magnetic bar suspended in liquid so it moves freely, always settling with the red end to north.
▸Some needles are luminous, which helps in the dark.
The three parts you can see moving

slides.label: Arrow index orienting scale
slides.notes: The index line is the one cadets miss and it is the one they read every single bearing against. Get them to put a finger on it. Stress that it is an extension of the direction of travel arrow - same line, so the bearing you read is the direction the arrow points.
slides.html:
Parts of the compass
Arrow, index line, orienting lines, scale
▸Direction of travel arrow — fixed in the baseplate, points the way you want to go. The sides of the baseplate run parallel to it.
▸Index line — a fixed line on the baseplate, an extension of the direction of travel arrow. This is where you read the bearing you have set.
▸Orienting lines — inside the rotating housing, made to lie parallel with the eastings on the map. Often half red to show north.
▸Compass scale — a centimetre scale along the edge for measuring map distances.
The index line is where the bearing is read

slides.label: Care of the compass
slides.notes: Do the metal demonstration for real - it takes ten seconds and cadets never forget it. Keys, a knife, a belt buckle, a phone. Then ask what they habitually carry in their chest pocket. The small air bubble is normal; a large one means the fluid has gone and the needle will stick.
slides.html:
The compass
Looking after it
▸Stand clear of metal — it deflects the needle and gives you a false bearing. Something as small as a watch makes a difference.
▸Hold it as flat as you can so the needle swings freely.
▸Do not drop it or knock it about.
▸Store it away from other compasses and away from electrical kit.
▸A large air bubble in the housing means it needs replacing.
Try it now
Put a knife or a set of keys next to your compass and watch the needle move. Then remember what is in your pockets.

slides.label: Cardinal points
slides.notes: Quick-fire round the room: north east? south west? west? Do it until it is instant. Cadets who have to count round the dial will be too slow when they are cold and tired, and slow is where mistakes come from. North east is 045 - the one most often got wrong.
slides.html:
The compass
The cardinal points
Learn these cold. You should be able to give the bearing for any of the eight without stopping to think.
▸North — 000°
▸North east — 045°
▸East — 090°
▸South east — 135°
▸South — 180°
▸South west — 225°
▸West — 270°
▸North west — 315°

slides.label: Section: converting
slides.notes: This is the single most examinable thing in the outcome and the thing cadets most often get backwards. Slow right down here.
slides.html:
Part Two
Converting bearings
The map speaks grid. The compass speaks magnetic. This is the translation.

slides.label: Mag to grid get rid
slides.notes: Chant it with them, twice. Then test it cold: I have measured 100 degrees off the map and I am about to walk it - what do I set? 101. I have shot 100 degrees at a church and I want to plot it - what do I draw? 099. Do not move on until the whole room gets both.
slides.html:
Map and compass work
Mag to grid, GET RID · Grid to mag, ADD
Learn it as a chant. It is the only mnemonic in the course you genuinely have to know by heart.
▸Mag to grid — GET RID. Taking a bearing on the ground and plotting it? Subtract the variation.
▸Grid to mag — ADD. Measured a bearing on the map and about to walk it? Add the variation.
In Yorkshire
The variation was 1° west in 2020. Small — but get the direction of the correction wrong and you are out by double.

slides.label: Why convert
slides.notes: Tie this straight back to LO2. The variation is not a fudge factor - it is the angle between two genuinely different norths. Cadets who understand that stop forgetting the correction.
slides.html:
Map and compass work
Why you have to convert at all
▸Working from the map, you work in grid bearings.
▸Following the compass on the ground, you work in magnetic bearings.
▸Your compass has never heard of grid north.
▸So every time you cross between map and ground, you convert.

slides.label: Section: setting a heading
slides.notes: Signpost. Five steps, and they must be done in order. Have everyone follow along on their own map and compass as you go.
slides.html:
Part Three
Setting a compass heading
Map to ground: measure it on the paper, then walk it.

slides.label: Setting a heading 1-2
slides.notes: Two mistakes to watch for. First, turning the whole compass instead of just the capsule in step two - hold the baseplate down hard. Second, the orienting arrow pointing to the bottom of the map, which gives you a bearing 180 degrees out. Walk round and check every cadet.
slides.html:
Setting a heading
Place the compass, turn the capsule
1Pick your start and finish — here the triangulation point and the church. Lay the compass on the map with its long edge running through both points and the direction of travel arrow pointing the way you want to go. You do not need the map set for this.
2Hold the baseplate firmly in place and turn only the capsule, until the orienting lines lie parallel to the north–south grid lines and the orienting arrow points to the top of the map.
Long edge through both points; orienting lines along the grid

slides.label: Setting a heading 3
slides.notes: The original PowerPoint had an error here - it showed fifty degrees. Point that out, because a cadet who has seen the old slides will query it, and catching an error in the teaching material is good navigation habit. Then re-do the arithmetic together with the current variation off their own sheet.
slides.html:
Setting a heading
Read it, then add the variation
1The compass now reads the angle between grid north and your intended direction — here 44°. Read it at the index line.
2That is a grid bearing. To walk it you need a magnetic bearing, so grid to mag, add. Add the variation — one degree — and turn the housing to read 45°.
Note
The original slide showed 50°. The correct figure with a 1° variation is 45°.
44° grid becomes 45° magnetic

slides.label: Setting a heading 4-5
slides.notes: The instinct is to twist the compass until the needle lines up, which of course changes nothing. Say it as an order: feet move, compass does not. Get them all to do it standing up, facing different ways to start with, and watch the whole room rotate.
slides.html:
Setting a heading
Off the map, onto the ground
1Take the compass off the map and hold it level in front of you, direction of travel arrow pointing away from you.
2Turn your body, not the compass, until the magnetic needle sits inside the orienting arrow with the red end to north and to the red N on the housing. You are now oriented with your surroundings.
3The direction of travel arrow is now pointing at the church you want to walk to.
Turn your body until the needle seats in the orienting arrow

slides.label: ANIMATION Taking a Bearing
slides.notes: Run this after the three step slides, as the consolidation. It repeats the whole sequence at a pace cadets can follow. Then have them do it once more on their own maps with the animation paused on the final frame.
slides.html:
Animation · play now

The full sequence end to end — compass placed on the map, capsule turned to the grid, the bearing read at the index line, the variation added, then the body turned until the needle seats.

slides.label: Following the bearing
slides.notes: This is the technique that separates cadets who can navigate from cadets who own a compass. Get them to try both on the ground - nose-in-the-compass versus mark-to-mark - and they will feel the difference immediately. In poor visibility the mark may only be twenty metres away, and that is fine.
slides.html:
On the ground
Following the bearing
▸Hold the compass level and steady.
▸Check the red end of the needle is in line with the red N every single time you look at it.
▸Follow the direction of travel arrow.
▸Better: line the arrow up with something real ahead of you — a tree, a pylon, a tower — and walk to that. Then take a new mark.
Why pick a feature
Walking to a mark is far easier and far more accurate than staring at the compass every step of the way.

slides.label: Map to ground
slides.notes: Use this as the checkpoint. Ask the room to talk you through the whole sequence from memory with the picture up. If they can, move on to the reverse; if not, go back to the step slides.
slides.html:
Map to ground
Putting it together
Working from the map out to the ground
You have measured a bearing on the map, converted it, and walked it. That is map to ground.

slides.label: Section: ground to map
slides.notes: Flag the change of direction clearly. Same equipment, same skills, opposite order - and the opposite correction. Mag to grid, get rid.
slides.html:
Part Four
Ground to map
The other direction: shoot something you can see, then work back to the paper.

slides.label: Ground to map: taking it
slides.notes: Four steps and they are all done standing up. Give them a target in the room or out of the window and have everyone shoot it, then compare numbers. If the answers spread by more than a few degrees, look for metal - radiators, chairs, watches.
slides.html:
Ground to map
Taking the bearing
1Pick the feature on the ground you want a bearing to.
2Hold the compass steady and level.
3Point the direction of travel arrow straight at the feature.
4Turn the housing until the red end of the needle lines up with the red N.
That is your magnetic bearing
You can walk along it as it stands, or convert it to a grid bearing to plot it on the map.

slides.label: Ground to map: plotting
slides.notes: Note the difference from map-to-ground: here you rotate the whole compass, not just the capsule, because the bearing is already set. Emphasise the last phrase - one bearing gives you a line, not a point. That is the hook for resection.
slides.html:
Ground to map
Plotting it on the map
1Find your own position on the map and mark it.
2Convert: mag to grid, get rid. Subtract the variation.
3Lay the compass on the map, keeping the bearing set on the housing, and rotate the whole compass until the orienting lines are parallel to the eastings.
4The edge of the compass should run through your position — and now shows the bearing on the map. You are somewhere on that line.
You are somewhere on that line

slides.label: ANIMATION Ground to Map
slides.notes: Run this immediately after the plotting slide while the idea of a line is fresh. It makes the jump from one line to three lines to a triangle visible in a way the static diagram cannot.

slides.label: Resection
slides.notes: The example uses a hill, a trig point and a church. Insist on faint pencil - they will be rubbing these out. Ask why three lines are better than two: two lines always cross somewhere, and give you no warning if one of them is wrong. Three disagreeing lines tell you something is off.
slides.html:
Ground to map
Resection
Working out where you are from features you can identify. Two features gives an intersection; three is better — triangulation.
▸Pick two, ideally three, features you can identify on the map
▸Take a compass bearing to each in turn
▸Convert each one to a grid bearing
▸Plot all three as faint pencil lines
▸Where they cross you get a small triangle
▸Your position is in the middle of it
Three bearings, three lines, one small triangle

slides.label: Quick orientation
slides.notes: This is the LO1 skill of setting the map, now done properly with a compass instead of by eye. Three steps, five seconds. Tell them to do it every single time they take the map out - habit, not decision.
slides.html:
Quick orientation
Setting the map with a compass
1Lay the compass on the map.
2Line the edge of the compass and the orienting lines up with the eastings.
3Turn your body until the red end of the needle is in line with the red N on the housing.
Do this constantly
It takes five seconds and it stops most navigation errors before they start.
You and your map are now facing north

slides.label: Slope aspect: the idea
slides.notes: The beach ball is the whole lesson - use it. Ask them to point at the fall line in the room, on the sloping floor if there is one. The commonest error is picking a diagonal line down the slope rather than the steepest line, so labour the word straight.
slides.html:
Slope aspect
When there is nothing to see
In poor visibility, with no identifiable feature anywhere, you can take a bearing on the shape of the ground itself.
▸You are near a slope but unsure exactly where
▸Imagine a heavy beach ball at your feet
▸Nothing to deflect it — no rocks, no wind
▸Give it a push. Which way does it roll?
▸That direction is the fall line
▸Take your bearing on that
The fall line — straight down, not diagonally

slides.label: Slope aspect: the method
slides.notes: Be honest that this feels haphazard compared with shooting a church tower - the original lesson says so too. Its value is that it works when nothing else does. The ninety-degrees-to-the-contours test is the part to drill; get them to find three matching slopes on their extract.
slides.html:
Slope aspect
Working it back to the map
1Sight the compass along the fall line — straight downhill, not diagonally. That is your bearing on the slope aspect.
2Subtract the variation. You now have a grid bearing.
3Lay the compass on the map. Align an orienting line with a vertical grid line, orienting arrow to the top of the map.
4Now hunt for a slope on the map that matches: the baseplate should sit at 90° to the contour lines, straight down the slope.
5Expect some trial and error.
Its limits
On a long hill with the same aspect throughout this narrows you to a line, not a point. Wait for the shape of the slope to change and take a fresh bearing then.

slides.label: Back bearing
slides.notes: Quick drill: forward bearing 040, back bearing? 220. Forward 300? 120. Do several. Then the practical warning from the original lesson - take your back bearing on a fixed object, never on the rest of the group, because the group drifts with you and tells you nothing.
slides.html:
Back bearing
Checking you are still on line
A back bearing is the exact opposite of your forward bearing — 180° different — used to check you have not drifted.
▸Forward bearing under 180°? Add 180°
▸Forward bearing over 180°? Subtract 180°
▸Turn the housing through 180°
▸Keep the needle pointing north — now the white end seats in the orienting arrow
▸Sight back at something that does not move
Turn the housing 180°; the white end of the needle now seats in the orienting arrow

slides.label: Section: roamer and distance
slides.notes: Signpost. Two practical skills that cadets use constantly and are rarely taught properly: reading an accurate grid reference, and measuring a real distance.
slides.html:
Part Five
Grid references
and distance
The scales round the edge of your compass, and what they are for.

slides.label: The roamer
slides.notes: Eastings before northings, every time - along the corridor then up the stairs is the usual reminder. The scale mismatch is the killer: a 1:50000 roamer on a 1:25000 map gives an answer that looks perfectly reasonable and is wrong by hundreds of metres. Make them check the printing on the baseplate.
slides.html:
The roamer
A six-figure grid reference, properly
A roamer gives you an accurate six-figure reference instead of an estimate.
▸Round the edge of the compass are rulers and roamers for different map scales
▸Check the roamer matches your map scale
▸Place the corner of the correct roamer on the feature
▸Read where the scales cut the grid lines
▸Eastings first — the north–south lines
▸Always read the lowest figures, from the south-west corner
Read eastings first: 377 067

slides.label: ANIMATION Roamer and Distances
slides.notes: Run this between the roamer slide and the paper-edge slides, since it covers both. Pause on the grid reference frame and ask the room to read it out before the animation does.
slides.html:

The roamer placed on a feature and the six-figure reference read off digit by digit, then a paper edge used to measure a leg and laid against the map scale.

slides.label: Measuring distance 1
slides.notes: Simplest trick in navigation and the one cadets are most impressed by. Any straight edge will do - a map case, a compass edge, the corner of a ration packet. Do a worked example together and have them all get the same answer before moving on.
slides.html:
Measuring distance
The paper-edge method
1Lay a straight edge of paper on the map between the two features and mark both positions on it.
2Move the paper down to the scale bar at the bottom of the map and read off the real distance.
3The scale bar has the unit to the left of the zero divided into tenths — put your right-hand mark on a whole unit, and the left mark falls on the tenths.
Mark both features on a paper edge

slides.label: Measuring distance 2
slides.notes: Show why the scale bar is built that way - the extra divided unit to the left of zero exists precisely so you can read a fraction without arithmetic. Then set them two or three legs to measure against the clock.
slides.html:
Measuring distance
Reading it off the scale
Right-hand mark on a whole unit; read the tenths to the left of zero
The tenths to the left of the zero are what give you the precision.

slides.label: Section: GPS
slides.notes: Frame it as the payoff. Cadets who have just spent an hour on resection are about to find out that their phone does the same thing with satellites. That connection is the point of this section.
slides.html:
Part Six
How GPS works
Worth understanding — because it is doing exactly what you have just done by hand.

slides.label: How GPS works
slides.notes: The key idea is that a GPS receiver is a clock, not a compass. It measures time of flight and converts to distance. Ask why four satellites rather than three - the fourth fixes the receiver clock error, and it gives you altitude.
slides.html:
GPS
Thirty satellites, twenty thousand kilometres up
▸About 30 satellites orbit the Earth at 20,000 km.
▸Built by the US government for military navigation; now anyone with a receiver can use the signals.
▸Wherever you are, at least four satellites are visible at any time.
▸Each broadcasts its own position and the current time, over and over.
▸Your receiver times how long each signal took to arrive, and turns that into a distance.
The GPS constellation

slides.label: Trilateration
slides.notes: Land the last line hard - this is exactly the resection they did earlier, with satellites instead of a church and a trig point. Cadets who get that stop thinking of GPS as magic, which makes them much better at judging when not to trust it.
slides.html:
GPS
Trilateration
Know your distance from satellite A and you are somewhere on a circle. Do it for B and C and the circles cross at one place.
▸One satellite: you are on a circle
▸Two: down to two possible points
▸Three: one intersection
▸Your receiver uses spheres, not circles
▸More satellites above the horizon means better accuracy
▸This is resection with satellites
Three distances, three circles, one intersection — your receiver uses spheres

slides.label: ANIMATION How GPS Works
slides.notes: Run this to close the section. It makes the sphere idea far clearer than the flat diagram. Finish by asking what happens to the fix when one satellite drops below the horizon.

slides.label: Recap
slides.notes: These four are the assessment. Test them by doing, not by asking - hand a cadet a map and a target and watch. The commonest failures are the wrong direction of correction and turning the compass instead of the body.
slides.html:
Learning Outcome 3
Can you do these four things?
1
Name every part of the compass and say what the index line is for.
2
Measure a bearing off the map, convert it, and walk it.
3
Shoot a bearing on the ground, convert it, and plot it.
4
Read a six-figure grid reference with the roamer, and measure a leg against the map scale.
